units.title: Lung Volumes and Capacities Tables (TV/IRV/ERV/RV with Male-Female Split; IC/FVC/FRC/TLC Formulas) & Volume-Time Graph
units.sec: Lung Volumes and Capacities Tables (TV/IRV/ERV/RV with Male-Female Split; IC/FVC/FRC/TLC Formulas) & Volume-Time Graph
units.guide:
Lung volumes (p197): tidal volume 500 ml (5–7 mL/kg) is the air moving in and out during quiet breathing; IRV is M 3.3 L / F 1.8 L (maximum inspired after tidal inspiration); ERV is M 1.3 L / F 0.8 L (maximum expired after tidal expiration); RV is 1.2 L (remaining after forceful maximum expiration).
Lung capacities: IC 3.5 L = TV + IRV (0.5 + 3 L); FVC 4.5 L = TV + IRV + ERV (0.5 + 3 + 1 L), the air expired with maximum force after forceful maximal inspiration; FRC 2.2 L = ERV + RV (1 + 1.2 L) = 1/2 FVC, the air remaining after a normal expiration; TLC 5.7 L = FVC + RV (4.5 + 1.2 L).
Closing note: elastic recoil pressure of the system is zero, and the lung's elastic recoil is counter-balanced by expansion of the chest wall. The volume–time spirogram on the same page labels TV, IRV, ERV, RV, IC, FRC, VC and TLC.

units.title: Residual Volume Measurement (Plethysmography vs Obsolete Gas Methods), Spirometry Procedure/Disadvantage, FEV1/FVC & Obstructive-Restrictive-Vascular Disease Tree
units.sec: Residual Volume Measurement (Plethysmography vs Obsolete Gas Methods), Spirometry Procedure/Disadvantage, FEV1/FVC & Obstructive-Restrictive-Vascular Disease Tree
units.guide:
RV (p198) cannot be measured with a spirometer, and therefore neither can FRC or TLC. It is measured by total body plethysmography (photographed), closed-circuit helium dilution or open-circuit nitrogen washout — the last two are bracketed 'Obsolete (doesn't include trapped gas in closed airways/pneumothorax)'.
Spirometry measures volume and flow to plot volume–time and flow–volume graphs; it is physically demanding, so it is avoided after MI, stroke, strenuous activity or smoking. The procedure is maximal inspiration → blast of expiration (continuous exhalation for 15 s or minimum 6 s) → maximum inhalation. FVC is 4.5 L normally expired in 5–6 s and FEV1/FVC is ≥80% (4 L).
The disease tree splits into obstructive (COPD with chronic bronchitis, emphysema and small airway disease; asthma; cystic fibrosis; bronchiolitis; bronchiectasis), restrictive (intraparenchymal ILD; extraparenchymal neuromuscular — myasthenia gravis, Guillain-Barré — and chest wall — kyphoscoliosis, obesity, ankylosing spondylitis) and vascular (pulmonary HTN, pulmonary thromboembolism).

units.title: Obstructive Disease (Emphysema): Hyperinflation Phase I vs Air Trapping Phase II Table & Bronchodilator Reversibility Testing
units.sec: Obstructive Disease (Emphysema): Hyperinflation Phase I vs Air Trapping Phase II Table & Bronchodilator Reversibility Testing
units.guide:
Normal forceful expiration (p199) depends on a driving pressure (elastic recoil plus intrapleural pressure) exceeding airway pressure. In COPD the elastic recoil is low, so the lung inflates easily and becomes hyperinflated (Phase 1); driving pressure then falls below airway pressure, bronchioles collapse because they lack cartilage, airways are dynamically compressed and air is trapped (Phase 2).
Phase I: FVC normal, FEV1 ↓↓, FEV1/FVC ↓↓, RV ↑↑, TLC ↑↑, reversibility (−). Phase II: FVC ↓↓, FEV1 ↓↓↓, FEV1/FVC ↓↓, RV ↑↑, TLC normal, reversibility (−).
If FEV1/FVC < 0.7, bronchodilator reversibility is tested with salbutamol 100 mg × 4 puffs or ipratropium 40 mg × 4 puffs (as printed), repeating after 30 minutes; a rise of 200 mL plus >12% ((post FEV1 − pre FEV1)/pre FEV1) indicates reversibility and bronchial asthma, whereas FEV1/FVC < 0.7 indicates COPD.

units.title: Restrictive Lung Disease: Diffusion vs Ventilation Indices, Intraparenchymal vs Extraparenchymal Types & Vascular Lung Disease
units.sec: Restrictive Lung Disease: Diffusion vs Ventilation Indices, Intraparenchymal vs Extraparenchymal Types & Vascular Lung Disease
units.guide:
Restrictive/ILD physiology (p200): fibrosis deranges diffusion and ventilation; initially diffusion from alveolus to capillary fails, giving ↓DLCO with a normal FVC, and as disease progresses diffusion and ventilation both fall — FVC ↓↓↓, FEV1 ↓, FEV1/FVC normal or ↑, RV ↓↓, TLC ↓↓, DLCO ↓↓.
Intraparenchymal disease is a diffusion disorder (eg ILD) with ↓↓↓ DLCO; extraparenchymal disease is a ventilation disorder (↓↓↓ FVC) with normal diffusion, normal DLCO and normal RV. Pure inspiratory (neuromuscular) disorders such as myasthenia gravis give ↑↑ RV/TLC with ↓TLC; combined inspiratory and expiratory disorders such as kyphoscoliosis give a normal RV/TLC.
Vascular lung disease has normal FEV1, FVC and FEV1/FVC with an abnormal DLCO.

units.title: Small Airway Disease (mmEFR, Closing Volume/Fowler) & Flow-Volume Curve Patterns (Normal, Mild, Severe Obstruction, Restriction)
units.sec: Small Airway Disease (mmEFR, Closing Volume/Fowler) & Flow-Volume Curve Patterns (Normal, Mild, Severe Obstruction, Restriction)
units.guide:
Small airway disease (p201) has normal FEV1/FVC and normal FVC, so it cannot be diagnosed with a spirometer; the diagnostic abnormalities are ↓↓ maximal mid-expiratory flow rate (mmEFR, also FEF 25–75, the flow in the mid half of the manoeuvre) and ↑↑ closing volume, measured by the single-breath nitrogen/Fowler technique (obsolete) with nitrogen read in phase 4 and normally 10% of VC.
On the flow–volume curve the early portion is effort dependent (trachea, large airways) and the rest effort independent; FVC is the area under the curve.
Patterns: normal — PEFR with no coving; mild obstruction — late plateau, FVC preserved, PEFR mildly reduced, coving/scooping/dog-tail; severe obstruction — no plateau, FVC reduced, PEFR severely reduced, coving; restriction — normal plateau, FVC reduced, PEFR normal or mildly reduced, no coving.

units.title: Upper Airway Obstruction Patterns (Extrathoracic/Intrathoracic/Fixed), Neuromuscular & Parenchymal Loops, and GOLD Staging
units.sec: Upper Airway Obstruction Patterns (Extrathoracic/Intrathoracic/Fixed), Neuromuscular & Parenchymal Loops, and GOLD Staging
units.guide:
Upper airway obstruction (p202): variable extrathoracic obstruction flattens inspiration (vocal cord palsy, laryngeal tumour, goitre, obstructive sleep apnoea); variable intrathoracic obstruction flattens expiration (foreign body, tracheomalacia); fixed obstruction flattens both, expiration from high pleural pressure and inspiration from negative intrathoracic pressure (tracheal stenosis). Small loops are also drawn for neuromuscular weakness and restrictive parenchymal lung disease.
GOLD staging uses post-bronchodilator FEV1: stage I ≥80%, II <80% to 50%, III <50% to 30%, IV <30%.

units.title: DLCO: Definition, Normal Values, Alveolo-Capillary Membrane Layers, Advantages of CO, Procedure & Blood Volume Determinant
units.sec: DLCO: Definition, Normal Values, Alveolo-Capillary Membrane Layers, Advantages of CO, Procedure & Blood Volume Determinant
units.guide:
DLCO or transfer factor (p203) is the diffusing capacity of the lung for carbon monoxide — a measure of the lung's ability to transfer gas across the respiratory membrane. Normal is 20–30 mL/min/mmHg; 70–140% of predicted is normal physiology and severe disease is <40%.
The respiratory (alveolo-capillary) membrane has a surface area of 70 m² and thickness 0.2–0.5 µm, with six layers: I fluid and surfactants, II alveolar epithelium, III epithelial basement layer, IV interstitial space, V capillary basement membrane, VI capillary endothelium.
CO is advantageous because its affinity for Hb is 210 times that of oxygen, blood levels are negligible and it is diffusion- rather than perfusion-limited. The manoeuvre is a 4-second deep inspiration of 0.3% CO, a 10-second breath hold, then maximal forced expiration. Blood volume is the most important determinant: ↑ blood volume → ↑ Hb → ↑ CO binding → ↑ DLCO.

units.title: Conditions Raising/Lowering DLCO, False-Low DLCO Causes, Diffuse Alveolar Hemorrhage & DLCO Across Respiratory Disorders
units.sec: Conditions Raising/Lowering DLCO, False-Low DLCO Causes, Diffuse Alveolar Hemorrhage & DLCO Across Respiratory Disorders
units.guide:
Raised DLCO (p204): diffuse alveolar haemorrhage, polycythaemia, supine posture (↑ venous return), exercise, left-to-right shunting, obesity, pregnancy (↑ blood volume) and mild congestive heart failure. Lowered DLCO: anaemia (↓ blood volume) and pulmonary oedema (thick interstitium).
False-low DLCO is produced by high-flow oxygen (high oxyhaemoglobin) and by smoking (high carboxyhaemoglobin reducing Hb binding of CO). Diffuse alveolar haemorrhage from bleeding within the lungs, as in Goodpasture syndrome, raises DLCO; DLCO is used to diagnose bleomycin toxicity, pulmonary vasculitis and early ILD.
DLCO by disorder: asthma ↑↑ (pulmonary hyperaemia with preferential perfusion), emphysema ↓ (printed as ↑ volume/surface area ratio in alveoli), chronic bronchitis normal, intraparenchymal restrictive disease ↓↓↓ (thickened respiratory membrane), extraparenchymal restrictive disease normal, vascular disease ↓ (↓ blood reaching lungs with normal FEV1 and FVC).

units.title: Coefficient of Diffusion (Kco) & the Stepwise Approach to Evaluation of Lung Diseases Flowchart
units.sec: Coefficient of Diffusion (Kco) & the Stepwise Approach to Evaluation of Lung Diseases Flowchart
units.guide:
Kco (p205) = DLCO / lung volume. In restrictive disease the intraparenchymal pattern is ↓DLCO with ↓ lung volume giving a normal Kco, whereas the extraparenchymal pattern is normal DLCO with ↓ lung volume giving ↑Kco.
Approach flowchart: FEV1/FVC = 0.7 with normal FVC → obstructive disease → post-bronchodilator FEV1 (asthma vs COPD); FEV1/FVC normal or ↑ with ↓FVC → restrictive disease → DLCO, where ↓DLCO means intraparenchymal disease (ILD, normal Kco) and normal DLCO means extraparenchymal disease (↑Kco) → RV/TLC, raised indicating neuromuscular and normal indicating chest-wall disorders; normal FEV1/FVC, normal FVC and ↓DLCO indicate vascular lung disease or early ILD, with FEF 25–75 and closing volume boxed for small airway disease.
